newsitem.title: UK: UK retail banks unprepared for euro-Coopers survey.
newsitem.headline: UK retail banks unprepared for euro-Coopers survey.

text.p: The UK retail banking sector is significantly behind its Continental European competitors in preparations for introduction of the euro, Coopers & Lybrand said in a survey released on Thursday.
"Based on the results of the survey, UK banks have a lot to do over the next five years," David Sayer, Coopers & Lybrand's retail banking consultancy partner, said in a statement.
The survey revealed that Continental Europeans do not see UK banks as a threat "largely because they do not believe that the UK will join the European Monetary Union at its outset."

The survey, carried out in conjunction with EFMA (the European Financial Management and Marketing Association), included 22 banks from the UK, Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and France, representing 60-70 percent of the retail banking markets in these countries.

"Across all banks surveyed there are large differences in their preparedness. A third of respondents are already formulating solutions and developing plans for conversion, with a further minority already implementing plans," it said.
The survey said 14 percent had not yet started to think about the possible strategic impact of the euro.
"Across all respondents there is far greater emphasis on the implications for practical conversion and less on the strategic impact on retail banking activities."
The survey revealed that retail banking was still very isolated and domestic with a multitude of barriers limiting consumer usage of cross-border banking services.

"Barriers are already eroding but the euro will accelerate this process and competition will increase significantly across markets, both from foreign banks and non-bank entrants, facilitated by the acceleration of remote banking," it said.
It said the isolation of domestic European banking had resulted in significant variations in margins and service levels in different countries.
"UK margins are particularly high and will come under threat," it said.
The survey revealed that in response to emerging competition, banks were relying on a range of strategies, with most emphasising a low cost strategy and raising of their brand image.

It said the German banks were seen as the biggest threat by all other countries including the UK, despite the fact that only a few have stated their intuition of competing across borders via their direct banking operations.
